name: Deep conditioner / hair mask

image.caption: Mask of a woman with a large coil of plaited hair MET vs00.2.10

lead: A deep conditioner or hair mask is a richer conditioning product left on for around 20 to 30 minutes after washing. It makes dry, bleached or heat-styled hair softer, shinier and easier to comb, and the improvement shows right away.

Cationic surfactants bind to negatively charged hair and flatten the cuticle, fatty alcohols and silicones lubricate the fibre, and small proteins may enter the shaft. Hair is not living tissue, so conditioners coat it rather than repair it. Claims of repair and strengthening are common in advertising and have not been established in trials of the products.

paras: Applied after shampooing, left on for the stated time, sometimes with warmth to increase penetration, then rinsed out. People use it weekly or as needed on dry or damaged hair.
Generally sold as a cosmetic. Allergic reactions to ingredients are documented, including a case report of food allergy triggered by an egg-based hair mask. Residue left on the scalp can flake.

angle.text: People use a deep conditioner or hair mask on dry or damaged hair for softness and shine after a longer contact time. The improvement in feel and look is immediate but temporary, because these products coat the hair rather than repair it.

lead: A deep conditioner, also called a hair mask, is a thicker and more concentrated version of hair conditioner, applied after washing and left on for a longer period than ordinary rinse-out conditioner before being rinsed off. Wikipedia describes typical contact times of about 20 to 30 minutes and says these products are aimed at very dry or damaged hair [1].

Conditioners improve the feel, appearance and combability of hair mainly by reducing friction between fibres. Because hair consists of dead cells, they do not repair it biologically; they deposit material that coats the fibre and fills damaged areas of the cuticle [1]. Benefits such as repair and strengthening are widely advertised, but the Wikipedia article treats them as claims rather than established outcomes [1].
No clinical trials of deep conditioners as a product category were located. Laboratory studies of individual conditioning ingredients exist and are summarised below.

paras: Undamaged hair carries a lipid film that makes it water-repellent and low in friction. Weathering, bleaching, dyeing and heat styling strip this film and leave the hair more negatively charged and rougher [1]. Deep conditioners are intended for hair in that state, and are thicker and more concentrated than instant or creme rinses [1].
Wikipedia notes that heat is sometimes used with deep conditioners to increase penetration [1].

According to Wikipedia, conditioners act by at least one of three routes: neutralising the negative charge with cationic compounds, lubricating the cuticle, or diffusing small proteins into the hair shaft [1]. Common components include cationic surfactants such as cetrimonium chloride, fatty alcohols (cetyl and stearyl), silicones such as dimethicone, hydrolysed proteins, panthenol, humectants, acidifiers such as citric acid, and preservatives [1].
Hydrolysed protein effects are described as temporary [1]. Masks often add oils or plant extracts, which vary by brand.

Studies cited by Wikipedia are laboratory work on hair fibres rather than trials of deep conditioner products. Keratin peptides of about 221 and 2,577 daltons were reported to penetrate relaxed textured hair while a roughly 75,000 dalton fraction mostly remained on the surface, and certain polymer pretreatments reduced breakage during combing after hot flat-ironing [1]. Panthenol was reported to increase break stress and elastic modulus in one study [1].

Deep conditioners are cosmetic products. A French study estimating exposure to hair cosmetics included hair masks among eleven hair product types, using consumption data on frequency and amount per use [2]. A published case report describes food allergy induced by a hen egg hair mask, illustrating that food-derived ingredients in homemade or commercial masks can provoke allergic reactions in sensitised people [3]. Wikipedia notes that conditioner left on the scalp may dry and flake in a way resembling dandruff [4].

No studies found. No human trials of deep conditioners or hair masks as a product category were located. Related research is limited to ingredient-level laboratory studies [1] and exposure and safety reports [2][3].
